title: Empty Empathy Machines
author: Ben Riley
summary: Writing in the aftermath of two mass-violence tragedies, Ben Riley uses M.J. Crockett's distinction between thick and thin empathy to examine so-called empathy machines. Thin empathy is grounded in knowledge-that, held in the absence of direct experience, while thick empathy arises from phenomenal and interpersonal knowledge, the knowledge-how that comes from lived experience of a situation or a person. Riley applies this to education, noting that the American ideal of teachers holding thick empathy for students is culturally specific rather than universal, then turns to VR simulations and chatbots. He argues both can generate only thin empathy: VR because participants always know they can turn it off, and chatbots because, however fluent, they feel no obligation to help and cannot physically intervene. Weaving in his late mother's online life and the foreseeable tragedy of Adam Raine's death, Riley warns that the most cognitively vulnerable may turn to these tools when what they most need is a flesh-and-blood human who cares with thick empathy.
